blocks.text:
Every database, no matter how well tuned, has a ceiling on how many reads per second it can absorb before latency starts creeping up and eventually the whole thing falls over. A distributed cache exists to keep the vast majority of read traffic from ever reaching that database at all, by holding a fast, in-memory copy of the data people actually ask for most often. This is a fundamentally different kind of system than the durable, quorum-replicated key-value store discussed elsewhere in this course: a cache is allowed to lose data. If a cache node crashes and its contents vanish, that is a performance problem, a wave of temporary cache misses, not a correctness problem, because the database underneath it still holds the real, durable truth.

That single framing, speed and availability over durability, shapes every decision in this design. We are going to build a distributed, horizontally-scalable caching layer that sits in front of a database, supports the classic get, set, and delete operations, evicts data intelligently when it runs low on memory, and stays fast and available even when individual cache nodes fail.

["Get: retrieve a cached value by key, returning a clear miss if it is not present.","Set: store a value under a key, with an optional time-to-live.","Delete: explicitly remove a key from the cache.","Automatic eviction: when memory fills up, the cache automatically removes entries according to a configurable policy rather than simply rejecting new writes.","Horizontal scaling: the cache cluster can grow by adding nodes without a full outage or a full cold restart."]
items: Get: retrieve a cached value by key, returning a clear miss if it is not present.
Set: store a value under a key, with an optional time-to-live.
Delete: explicitly remove a key from the cache.
Automatic eviction: when memory fills up, the cache automatically removes entries according to a configurable policy rather than simply rejecting new writes.
Horizontal scaling: the cache cluster can grow by adding nodes without a full outage or a full cold restart.

Staleness tolerance: the system explicitly accepts that cached data can be briefly out of date in exchange for speed.

items: The cache supports simple key-value get, set, and delete, with values up to a few hundred kilobytes.
Cache-aside is the default pattern used by application code, with write-through and write-back available as opt-in alternatives for callers with different durability-versus-latency needs.
The cache is primarily in-memory with no strong persistence guarantee; a full cluster restart is expected to start cold and repopulate from the database over time.
This design covers a single-region deployment, with multi-region caching noted as a future extension.
Eviction defaults to LRU, with LFU and TTL-based expiration available as configurable alternatives.

blocks.text: Consider an application with a total read volume of 500,000 requests per second against its primary data store, and suppose the caching layer achieves a healthy 92 percent hit ratio. That means 500,000 times 0.92, or about 460,000 requests per second are served entirely by the cache, and only 500,000 minus 460,000, roughly 40,000 requests per second actually reach the database. That difference, an order of magnitude reduction in database load, is the entire economic and performance justification for building this layer in the first place.

blocks.text: A request for cached data first checks a small, local L1 cache living in the application process itself, then falls back to the larger, shared L2 distributed cache cluster, and only falls all the way through to the database on a genuine full miss. The cluster itself is not one giant cache, it is many smaller shard nodes, each owning a slice of the keyspace via consistent hashing.

blocks.title: Why the API returns an explicit miss rather than null
blocks.text: A stored value that happens to be null or empty needs to be distinguishable from "this key was never cached at all," otherwise application code cannot correctly tell the difference between "the cache says this value is genuinely absent" and "the cache simply does not have an opinion, go check the database." An explicit miss indicator, separate from the value itself, avoids that entire class of subtle bug.

blocks.text: Internally, each cache node organizes its data as a hashmap for O(1) key lookup, paired with a doubly linked list ordered by recency of access, the classic structure behind an efficient LRU implementation.

blocks.text: As with the distributed key-value store, consistent hashing governs how keys map to shard nodes, so that adding or removing a cache node only requires rebalancing a small fraction of the keyspace rather than a full reshuffle. The important difference in framing here: losing a shard in this system means a temporary wave of cache misses for the keys it owned, not lost data, since the database remains the durable source of truth underneath. That relaxed risk posture is exactly why a cache cluster can run leaner, with less replication overhead, than a database cluster serving the same key space would need.

A worked example sequence diagram: Alice requests a profile page causing a cache miss and database read that populates the cache, and Bob requesting the same profile moments later gets a fast cache hit

blocks.text: Alice opens a profile page that has not been viewed by anyone recently. The application checks the cache, gets a miss, reads the profile from the database, populates the cache with that value, and returns it to Alice, the whole round trip dominated by that one database read. Thirty seconds later, Bob opens the exact same profile. This time the cache check is a hit, and the response comes back an order of magnitude faster, with the database never touched at all for Bob's request. That difference, repeated across millions of requests a day for popular content, is the entire value proposition of this layer made concrete.

blocks.alt: A cache-aside pattern diagram showing a read checking the cache, falling back to the database on a miss, and populating the cache afterward

blocks.text: The application code explicitly checks the cache first and manages populating it on a miss. This is the most common pattern because it is simple and resilient: if the cache is entirely down, reads still work, just slower, falling through to the database every time.
blocks.content: The application code explicitly checks the cache first and manages populating it on a miss. This is the most common pattern because it is simple and resilient: if the cache is entirely down, reads still work, just slower, falling through to the database every time.

blocks.alt: A write through pattern diagram showing a write going to the cache and then synchronously to the database before acknowledging success

blocks.text: Every write updates the cache and the database together, synchronously, before returning success. This guarantees the cache is never stale relative to what was just written, at the cost of every write paying the full latency of the database write, not just the cache write.
blocks.content: Every write updates the cache and the database together, synchronously, before returning success. This guarantees the cache is never stale relative to what was just written, at the cost of every write paying the full latency of the database write, not just the cache write.

blocks.alt: A write back pattern diagram showing a write hitting the cache immediately and being acknowledged right away, with the database write happening asynchronously later

blocks.text: A write lands in the cache and is acknowledged to the caller immediately, with the database update happening asynchronously afterward. This is the fastest write path by far, but it carries real durability risk: if the cache node crashes before that asynchronous flush happens, the write is lost entirely, which makes this pattern appropriate only for data where that risk is genuinely acceptable.

blocks.text: LRU (least recently used) evicts whatever has not been accessed in the longest time, implemented efficiently with the hashmap-plus-linked-list structure from section 10. LFU (least frequently used) evicts based on access count rather than recency, which better protects consistently popular items from a temporary burst of unrelated traffic, at the cost of needing to track and maintain frequency counts, more bookkeeping than LRU requires. TTL-based expiration removes entries after a fixed time regardless of access pattern, simplest of all, and often layered on top of LRU or LFU rather than used entirely alone.

blocks.text: Write-back's asynchronous flush to the database, and pub-sub invalidation broadcasts across cache layers, are the two genuinely async workloads in this system. Both benefit from a durable queue in front of them so a temporary downstream slowdown (a busy database, a slow cache node) does not directly translate into dropped writes or missed invalidations.

blocks.alt: Application servers routed by a shard router to the correct cache shard

blocks.text: Because every key has exactly one correct shard owner via consistent hashing, "load balancing" here is really about even key distribution across shards (helped by virtual nodes, the same technique used in the distributed key-value store design) rather than arbitrary request routing.

blocks.alt: A flowchart showing a shard being added to the ring once memory utilization crosses a target threshold

blocks.text: Adding a shard to the ring redistributes a small, bounded slice of keys to the new node, the same consistent-hashing benefit seen elsewhere. Unlike a durable database, a newly added cache shard can start completely empty and simply warm up naturally as requests for its newly-owned keys come in and miss, populate, and get cached going forward.

blocks.text: This section is worth addressing directly by contrast: the "database" being scaled here is the cache cluster itself, and it scales purely by adding shards, since there is no durability-driven replication factor to reason carefully about the way there would be for the actual source-of-truth database sitting behind this cache. Light replication (one replica per shard) exists purely to reduce how often a single node failure causes a burst of cache misses, not to guarantee data survival.

blocks.alt: A diagram showing the choice of availability over strict consistency, justified by the fact that losing a cache node means slower reads, not wrong data, since the database remains the source of truth

blocks.text: This is close to the easiest CAP-theorem call in the entire course. A cache almost always chooses availability, because the worst-case failure mode, a stale or missing cache entry, degrades gracefully into "slightly slower, but still correct" rather than "wrong." The database underneath remains the actual source of truth, and the cache is free to be wrong, briefly, exactly because something else is always there to fall back on.

blocks.alt: A cache shard with a read replica, and the database still holding the source of truth if the shard fails entirely

blocks.text: When a shard fails, its keys simply become misses until the shard (or its replica) recovers, and every one of those misses falls through cleanly to the database, exactly as designed. This is a fundamentally simpler failure story than the durable key-value store's hinted-handoff-and-anti-entropy-repair machinery, precisely because correctness was never on the line here to begin with.

blocks.text: Cache traffic should run over an encrypted internal network segment, and access should be restricted to the application servers that legitimately need it, since a cache frequently holds copies of sensitive data (user sessions, personal profile fields) even though it is not the durable system of record for that data. Standard authentication between application servers and the cache cluster prevents an unauthorized process from reading or poisoning cached values.

blocks.text: Cache hit ratio is the single most important metric in this entire system, full stop. A sustained drop in hit ratio is often the very first visible symptom of a much bigger problem elsewhere, a cache node that silently died, a deploy that changed key naming and broke lookups, a traffic pattern shift toward less cacheable content. Per-shard latency, eviction rate, and memory utilization round out the picture, and a sudden spike in eviction rate specifically flags that the working set has outgrown current cluster capacity.

blocks.alt: A map of two bottlenecks: a single extremely hot key overwhelming its shard, fixed by request coalescing plus a local L1 cache, and a cold cache after a full cluster restart, fixed by gradual warm up with the database absorbing temporary extra load

blocks.text: The defining bottleneck in any distributed cache is the hot key problem: consistent hashing guarantees even distribution of the keyspace, but says nothing about even distribution of access frequency. A single viral item can generate enough traffic to overwhelm the one shard that happens to own it, even while every other shard sits comfortably idle.

blocks.alt: A diagram showing thousands of requests for one viral key being absorbed by request coalescing (one shared fetch for all concurrent waiters) and a local L1 cache reducing repeat traffic to the shared cluster

blocks.text: Request coalescing ensures that if a thousand requests for the same missing key arrive within milliseconds of each other, only one of them actually goes and fetches the value, with the other 999 simply waiting on that first fetch's result, rather than triggering a thousand redundant database reads. The local L1 cache layer from section 7 compounds this protection further, since it absorbs a meaningful fraction of repeat reads for a hot key before they ever reach the shared cluster at all.

blocks.text: The three caching patterns from section 14 form a genuine spectrum: cache-aside is the simplest and most resilient to a fully down cache, at the cost of every miss paying full database latency; write-through keeps the cache always fresh at the cost of every write being as slow as the database; write-back is the fastest for writes by far, at the cost of a real durability risk if the cache fails before flushing. Most real systems use different patterns for different data, cache-aside for read-heavy, rarely-written data, write-back only for data where losing the last few seconds of writes on a crash is genuinely tolerable.

blocks.alt: A comparison of TTL expiration, the simplest invalidation approach, explicit invalidation on write, and pub sub broadcast invalidation across multiple cache layers

blocks.text: TTL expiration requires no coordination at all and is trivially simple, at the cost of data staying stale for up to the full TTL window after a real update happens. Explicit invalidation on write keeps data fresher, at the cost of the write path now needing to know about and reach every cache layer holding a copy. Pub-sub invalidation broadcasts that same invalidation out to potentially many cache layers, including local L1 caches spread across an entire fleet of application instances, solving the multi-layer freshness problem at the cost of running an additional messaging system.

blocks.alt: A cost breakdown dominated by memory, which is expensive per gigabyte, with compute being a comparatively minor cost

blocks.text: Memory is expensive, meaningfully more so per gigabyte than disk-based database storage, so right-sizing the cluster against the actual working set (not simply over-provisioning generously) is the primary cost lever here. Choosing a shorter default TTL for less-critical data, and being deliberate about which data actually earns a place in the cache at all rather than caching indiscriminately, both directly reduce the memory footprint needed.

["A full cluster restart leaves every shard cold simultaneously, causing a temporary spike in database load as the cache rewarms from scratch, worth planning capacity headroom for.","A write-back write is lost when a cache node crashes before its asynchronous flush completes, which the design accepts as a known, bounded risk for that specific pattern.","A hot key so extreme that even request coalescing and a local L1 cache cannot fully absorb it, at which point the underlying data may genuinely need to be restructured (denormalized, precomputed) rather than solved purely at the caching layer.","A shard rebalance after adding a node causes a brief wave of misses for the specific keys that moved, which is expected and self-resolving as they repopulate."]
items: A full cluster restart leaves every shard cold simultaneously, causing a temporary spike in database load as the cache rewarms from scratch, worth planning capacity headroom for.
A write-back write is lost when a cache node crashes before its asynchronous flush completes, which the design accepts as a known, bounded risk for that specific pattern.

A hot key so extreme that even request coalescing and a local L1 cache cannot fully absorb it, at which point the underlying data may genuinely need to be restructured (denormalized, precomputed) rather than solved purely at the caching layer.
A shard rebalance after adding a node causes a brief wave of misses for the specific keys that moved, which is expected and self-resolving as they repopulate.

codes.python:
import threading
from concurrent.futures import Future
from typing import Callable, Dict, Generic, TypeVar

V = TypeVar("V")


# Ensures that if many callers request the same missing key at nearly the
# same moment, only one of them actually performs the expensive fetch,
# while the rest share that single fetch's result.
class HotKeyCoalescer(Generic[V]):
    def __init__(self):
        self._in_flight: Dict[str, "Future[V]"] = {}
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def fetch(self, key: str, loader: Callable[[], V]) -> "Future[V]":
        with self._lock:
            if key in self._in_flight:
                return self._in_flight[key]
            future: "Future[V]" = Future()
            self._in_flight[key] = future

        def run() -> None:
            try:
                result = loader()
                future.set_result(result)
            finally:
                with self._lock:
                    self._in_flight.pop(key, None)

        threading.Thread(target=run, daemon=True).start()
        return future
